doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Why the white and black records sound different; Louis Armstrong
summary: Mancuso discusses melodic versus hot styles, race, and Louis Armstrong's energy and chops.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Because in class I just play his last five notes, and then we listen to the great solo of “Singing the Blues” by Bix. And then I do Vince Giordano replicating it a hundred years later and everything.
Why in your estimation are those records so different?

It might be because it was such a separation of white and black. And the cool nature of some of the players, which they didn’t call cool at the time, but there was a more melodic kind of approach. And it had to do with race at the time but there were some great, hot players who were white. But to me, Bix, I love that stuff. And I love Louis’ stuff. The King Oliver stuff was a little, I don’t think I’d say sloppy, but it was different. And there was a certain kind of articulation that some of these guys brought into the music. And some of the historians took them to task for it, but then you have a genius like Louis. I mean he just, he just cut right through a lot of that stuff.
Yeah. It was just amazing what he did.
It’s funny, how could you criticize a style that was developing. It’s like they’re criticizing it because it didn’t end up where Louis took it.
They set him up, it’s like they set him up to blow it up.

Yeah. And plus he had the great chops, you know, he’s going to hit these high C’s and he had the energy to lift a God damn rocket ship. So why not? I mean the guy — you know I show them the clip of him doing one of these songs, and I go, “This guy was smoking weed before every show, and it’s supposed to be mellow. You know, I mean look at him. He can’t even stand still. He just can’t wait to take a solo. He’s just so full of energy and imagination.” And we’re all richer for it.
